claims.text: Heating Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu HEA nanoparticles induces element-dependent atomic diffusion.
Elements with higher melting points preferentially segregate into the nanoparticle sub-surface during heating.
Elements with higher relative surface energies can occupy sub-surface positions and stabilize surface atoms.
Sub-surface segregation produces a passivating shell that delays complete melting.
The initially solid Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu nanoparticles are homogeneous solid solutions.
ML-enhanced atomistic simulations can represent diffusion and particle relaxation sufficiently to enable sub-surface migration and segregation.
The proposed comparison holds nanoparticle size and composition similar while varying whether diffusion is allowed or suppressed.
In the relevant premelting regime, diffusion and particle relaxation can compete with melting kinetics.
The segregated shell is expected to be enriched in Ni, Cr, or Co.
Local coordination and dissolution potential determine which atoms stabilize low-coordination surface positions.
Differential diffusion during heating drives stabilizing elements into sub-surface positions.
The resulting shell resists premelting-induced structural disorder.
Pronounced sub-surface segregation will delay melting onset and raise the effective melting temperature relative to homogeneous particles.
Segregated particles will maintain their shape better or exhibit less coalescence than homogeneous baseline particles.
The baseline consists of otherwise comparable HEA nanoparticles that undergo little or no sub-surface segregation.
The proposed mechanism applies only over a particle-size and heating-rate range in which diffusion and relaxation can compete with melting.
The mechanism may fail at extreme heating rates or for substantially different compositions exhibiting bulk-dominated behavior.
Diffusion rates, melting-point shifts, and segregation profiles are uncertain and sensitive to simulation, synthesis, and experimental conditions.
If diffusion-suppressed and segregation-permitted particles have indistinguishable melting onsets and morphological evolution, the proposed segregation-controlled mechanism is falsified.
